entities.summary:
Aristokles (c. 600 – c. 560 BCE), a foundational Athenian sculptor, emerged during the late Archaic period, a pivotal era witnessing the transition from rigid, stylized forms to more naturalistic representations in Greek art. Active primarily in Attica, he is recognized as a progenitor of a distinguished lineage of sculptors, including his sons Kanachos and Ageladas, whose collective contributions significantly shaped the trajectory of early Classical sculpture. His work, often in marble and bronze, served both public and private commissions, reflecting the burgeoning artistic patronage and civic pride of Athenian society as it moved towards democratic ideals. Aristokles’ significance lies in his role in establishing the stylistic groundwork for the subsequent generations of Athenian artists who would define the Golden Age of Greek art.

While specific works definitively attributed solely to Aristokles are scarce due to the passage of time and the nature of ancient artistic traditions, his name is associated with the early development of the kouros and kore types, along with architectural sculpture. He is believed to have contributed to the sculptural programs of significant sanctuaries and public buildings, where his mastery of anatomical detail and increasingly dynamic poses would have been evident. The stylistic innovations attributed to his workshop included a greater emphasis on the human form's musculature and a move away from the purely frontal, static compositions characteristic of earlier Archaic art, laying the groundwork for the 'Severe Style' that would soon follow.
